newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to form its own elite combat unit.
newsitem.headline: Germany to form its own elite combat unit.

text.p: The head of Germany's land forces on Thursday unveiled detailed plans for a 1,000-strong special combat unit along the lines of Britain's legendary SAS.

The elite unit, geared to behind-the-lines operations and freeing hostages abroad, is part of a broad reform designed to give Germany a rapid response capability which it never needed in four decades of Cold War.

"This will certainly be a very elite unit with special abilities and tasks of a classic military nature -- disrupting enemy communications behind the lines and gathering intelligence," Lieutenant-General Helmut Willmann told reporters.

The formation of the new KSK or Special Forces Unit is another example of how Germany is shedding post-war reluctance to contemplate fighting abroad -- something which has come more easily to former colonial powers like Britain and France.
"I have told our officers we need to define mission-readiness in a different way," Willmann said.
"There is not the same need to be ready to mobilise our forces within 48 hours to defend ourselves against an invasion."

Instead, Germany -- which helped to bankroll the 1991 Gulf War rather than send its own troops -- has found its allies calling on it to play an increasingly full role in a range of multinational missions such as peacekeeping in Bosnia.
Only two years ago, an embarrassed Germany had to rely on Belgian soldiers to evacuate trapped German citizens from Rwanda as civil war was breaking out.
"It's a sorry state of affairs when a nation of our size has to ask the paratroops of a small friendly country to free German citizens," Willmann said.
Such operations will soon also be the province of the KSK, which will be equipped with the best weaponry on offer, including high-velocity rifles and night-vision equipment.
All the soldiers will have to pass a gruelling 10-day selection procedure including a 90-km (55-mile) footmarch in combat conditions, and then undergo a three-month trial period.
Training will last three years and produce specialised units for operations including parachute and waterborne landings.
Germany will cooperate with the British Special Air Services (SAS) and is sending its first batch of soldiers to train in Britain in the next few months.
Because of the need to build the force from scratch, it will not reach full strength until the year 2000.
Overall, Germany aims to have around 37,000 troops available for all kinds of rapid deployment by the turn of the century.

By October next year it expects to have some 10,000 soldiers trained up so that it could, at short notice, send a task force of between 4,000 and 5,000 troops to carry out humanitarian missions and evacuations in crisis areas.
